title: Entropy-Driven Initiation and Cellular Uptake Mediated by Viscoelastic Cytoskeleton: A Kinetic Phase Diagram from Onsager Variational Principle
authors: Jinjie Liu, Zhong-Can Ou-Yang, Hao Wu
abstract: A fundamental question in receptor-mediated endocytosis remains unanswered: what initial driving force brings ligands and receptors into close proximity? While previous models assume pre-existing contact and overlook this initiation problem, we propose that entropic forces from nanoscale biomolecules in crowded cellular environments provide the essential driving mechanism. We develop a unified continuum model rooted in the Onsager variational principle, where engulfment depth serves as the generalized coordinate and the driving force derives from a free energy landscape of entropic, binding, membrane, and cytoskeleton contributions. The framework naturally incorporates: (i) entropy-driven adhesion as initiation; (ii) ligand-receptor binding as the sustaining force; (iii) membrane deformation via the Helfrich-Canham Hamiltonian; and (iv) cytoskeleton viscoelasticity through the elastic-viscoelastic correspondence principle. The kinetic phase diagram predicts a critical biomolecule concentration for initiation, a lower bound of ligand density for complete engulfment, a finite size window for engulfable particles, and an optimal virus radius of 30--60 nm that decreases with increasing binding energy. The Onsager solubility condition naturally yields the phase boundaries. The model exhibits asymptotic consistency with the classic Asakura-Oosawa result in the large-particle flat-surface limit. Stiffer cells lead to longer engulfment times and narrower size windows. Strikingly, the optimal size matches HIV-1 dimensions under physiologically realistic parameters. This work provides a variational foundation for cellular uptake with implications for virology, nanotechnology, and drug delivery.
summary: This work develops a comprehensive continuum model using the Onsager variational principle to explain cellular engulfment. It uniquely posits that entropic depletion forces provide the necessary initial 'push' before specific receptor binding sustains the process. The resulting kinetic phase diagram offers quantitative predictions for successful viral uptake, linking fundamental physics principles to virology and nanomedicine.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental, unanswered question of the initial driving force required for ligands and receptors to approach each other during receptor-mediated endocytosis.
main_result: It predicts a kinetic phase diagram defining critical biomolecule concentrations and optimal particle sizes (e.g., 30–60 nm) necessary for successful cellular engulfment.
method: The authors develop a unified continuum model rooted in the Onsager variational principle to derive the kinetics from a total free energy landscape incorporating multiple physical contributions.
model_or_system: The system models viral or nanoparticle uptake by a cell membrane, treating the process as having distinct phases: initial entropy-driven approach (depletion forces), followed by sustained binding and viscoelastic cytoskeletal deformation.
key_observables: Kinetic phase diagram, critical biomolecule concentration ($c_{crit}$), optimal virus radius ($R_{opt}$), and engulfment time $t(h)$.
important_parameters: Membrane tension ($\gamma$), Young's moduli ($E_v, E_m$), viscosity coefficients ($\mu, \eta_m$), and biomolecule concentration ($c$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes the use of the Onsager variational principle for dynamics, employs the Helfrich-Canham Hamiltonian for membrane bending, and models cytoskeleton viscoelasticity using a linear solid approximation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate depletion-driven engulfment mechanisms, showing how entropic forces stabilize uptake mediated by the cytoskeleton across different stages of contact.
paper_structure: The paper builds from identifying the initiation problem to developing a unified free energy functional (summing entropy, binding, membrane, and cytoskeleton terms). It then applies the Onsager principle to derive the kinetic equation, culminating in phase diagram predictions and size optimization criteria.
why_interesting: While focused on biophysics, the rigorous application of variational principles (Onsager) to couple multiple dissipative/restoring forces (viscoelasticity, entropy) provides a powerful theoretical template for analyzing non-equilibrium dynamics in complex soft matter systems relevant to AMO physics.
